newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil moves to limit import financing.
newsitem.headline: Brazil moves to limit import financing.

text.p: Brazil, facing a widening trade gap, clamped down Tuesday on short-term financing of imports by making importers pay for their foreign currency on the day they pick their goods up from the warehouse.

Gustavo Franco, Central Bank Director of International Affairs, said the new conditions for imports with less than 360-day financing could affect up to 65 percent of all overseas purchases but he was convinced the move was "not protectionist".
"This equalises the treatment of imports and exports," Franco said. "I'm convinced this is nothing protectionist as it only affects the capital account."

The new rules, to be published in Wednesday's Official Journal and which come into force for goods shipped after March 31, were announced on the same day Brazil revealed its trade deficit for the year so far had reached some $2.8 billion.
Franco said the credit limits would naturally affect the trade balance but "it would not be significant".
More significant was the simple removal of "incentives" for imports that "distorted" the competitiveness of national products.

Imports with less than 180 days financing must take out foreign exchange contracts the day the goods are picked up from customs, with 100 percent of the contract being paid in cash. Importers can make credit arrangements with banks.

Imports financed for 180-360 days must have foreign exchange contracts taken out 180 days before payment falls due. Every day importers fail to pay up or to obey the foreign exchange contracting rules, they will be fined.

Long-term financing of more than 360 days is exempt from the conditions, as are fuel and lubricant imports by state oil firm Petrobras, imports worth less than $10,000 and some imports carried out under so-called "drawback" arrangements.

"The idea is to equalise the treatment of imports and exports when it comes down to capital flows," Franco said, noting there had been restrictions on export financing for some time and punishments for delayed payments on overseas sales.
"Many imports were simply happening because of the financing that went with them," he said.
Franco said 25 percent of imports were paid in cash, 10 percent had long-term financing and 65 percent fell in between.
